theme: The Assyrian crisis; Hezekiah’s prayer; Sennacherib falls
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 36:1-37:38. This is the same story you read in 2 Kings 18-19, now from Isaiah’s side. Notice what is added: the sharpness of the Assyrian propaganda, the detail of Hezekiah’s prayer, and the poem that Isaiah speaks against Sennacherib.
settingTheScene: Isaiah 36-39 is a historical interlude that connects the two halves of the book. It repeats and expands the account in 2 Kings, with an important addition in Isaiah 38. In 701 BC, Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem after capturing the other cities of Judah. He sent his field commander to demoralize the city. This is the pivotal event of the first half of Isaiah: will the nation trust in God or in the powers of the world?
observation: “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you” (36:14).
“Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?” (36:20).
“This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace” (37:3).
“O LORD of hosts, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth” (37:16).
“Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see” (37:17).
“Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice?” (37:23).
“And the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians” (37:36).
interpretation:
The field commander speaks like a skilled propagandist. He begins by undermining confidence in Egypt, then in Hezekiah, then in the LORD. He says that Hezekiah removed the altars of the LORD, which he distorts as an insult to God, though it was a reform. He claims that the LORD told him to attack Judah. And his final argument is the most dangerous: no god of any nation has saved it from Assyria, so why would the LORD? It places the LORD on the same level as the idols of the nations. It is a claim that God is no different from other gods, and it has to be answered.

Hezekiah’s response is quiet. The army is ordered not to answer. The king goes to the house of the LORD and sends for the prophet. Isaiah gives the first word: “Do not be afraid.” Then Sennacherib sends a second letter, and Hezekiah does the thing for which he is remembered. He spreads it out before the LORD. His prayer is a model. It begins with who God is: enthroned above the cherubim, the only God of all the kingdoms, the maker of heaven and earth. It describes the threat honestly. It makes a request: save us. And it states the purpose: “that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD.”

God’s answer through Isaiah is a poem of mockery against the proud king. “Whom have you mocked and reviled?” It was against the Holy One of Israel. The king thinks he has conquered by his own power, but God says, “Have you not heard that I determined it long ago?” Assyria was an instrument, and its pride is its downfall. God promises to put his hook in Sennacherib’s nose and turn him back the way he came.

That night the angel of the LORD strikes down 185,000 in the camp. In the morning, the army is dead. Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, and years later he is killed by his own sons while worshiping his god. The god he trusted could not protect him.
connection: Jesus told his disciples to pray in his name and promised that the Father would give what they asked (John 16:23-24). Hebrews 4:16 invites us to the throne of grace. 2 Corinthians 10:4-5 says our weapons are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds. Psalm 46 and Psalm 48, coming up, celebrate this deliverance. Revelation 12:11 says the saints conquer by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony.
application:
Use Hezekiah’s prayer as a pattern: begin with who God is, bring the problem honestly, make your request, and state your purpose.

When voices tell you that no one can help you, remember the 185,000.

Write down a problem and, as Hezekiah did, spread it before the LORD.
prayerPrompts: Spread before God what troubles you, as Hezekiah did.
Ask him to incline his ear and open his eyes.
Praise him as the God, you alone.
